opus-5.5.text:
I think of them as complementary rather than competing, and each one is good at something the others aren't.

Real-robot data is the ground truth. It's collected on the actual embodiment, with the actual sensors, the actual latency, and all the messy contact physics that's really hard to model. If you want a policy to work on a specific robot in the real world, there's no substitute for some amount of data from that robot. The problem is that it's expensive and slow. You need hardware, operators, resets, maintenance, and it doesn't scale the way internet data does. So I see real-robot data as the high-value, low-volume part of the mix, the thing you use to anchor and fine-tune.

Simulation is almost the opposite. It's cheap, it's parallelizable, you can generate huge amounts of experience, and you can do things like reinforcement learning that would be impractical or unsafe on hardware. It's been very successful for locomotion and for certain dexterous tasks where the dynamics can be reasonably modeled. But for contact-rich manipulation, deformable objects, and long-horizon tasks in diverse environments, the sim-to-real gap is still real, and building diverse, realistic scenes and assets is its own bottleneck. So simulation is great for scale and for exploring behaviors, but you have to be honest about where it doesn't transfer.

Human hand data, things like handheld grippers, gloves, or just video of people doing tasks, sits in an interesting middle ground. It's much cheaper to collect than teleoperated robot data, you can take it into homes and all kinds of places, and it captures how people actually solve tasks, which is a very rich source of priors. The challenge is the embodiment gap. A human hand isn't a robot gripper, and the kinematics, the forces, even the camera viewpoint differ. A lot of the recent work is really about designing interfaces or representations that make human data more directly usable by robots.

So the way I'd put it is like a pyramid: large amounts of diverse but less directly aligned data at the bottom, human video and simulation, which help with generalization and understanding of the world; then more aligned data like human demonstrations through robot-like interfaces; and at the top a smaller amount of real-robot data that closes the last gap to deployment. The interesting research question isn't which one wins, it's how to combine them so that each type of data is doing the job it's best at.

r001.rationale: The response says human-hand data is cheaper to collect and can be collected in homes, but it does not compare this with bringing robots into those homes.

r002.rationale: The response says real-robot data is necessary for a policy to work on a specific robot in the real world and that it closes the final gap to deployment.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. I think the honest answer is that none of the three is sufficient on its own, and the interesting question is how you sequence them.

Real-robot data is the ground truth. It captures the actual dynamics, the sensor noise, the contact behavior that you simply cannot fake. The problem is cost. Every hour of teleoperation requires a robot, an operator, a lab, and someone to reset the scene when things go wrong. You end up with datasets that are precious but small, and often biased toward whatever tasks were easy to set up that week.

Simulation sits at the opposite end. It is nearly free to scale, you can randomize everything, and you can generate failure cases that would be dangerous or tedious to collect physically. But the sim-to-real gap is still very much alive, especially for anything involving deformable objects, friction, or fine contact. I have seen policies that look flawless in simulation fall apart the moment a cable has slightly different stiffness than the model assumed. So I treat simulation as a way to learn structure and priors, not as a replacement for touching the world.

Then there is human hand data, meaning people wearing gloves or cameras and doing tasks directly, without a robot in the loop at all. This is where I have become most optimistic recently. Humans are extraordinarily efficient demonstrators. You can collect thousands of diverse manipulation examples in a day in real homes and kitchens, with real objects and real clutter. The catch is the embodiment gap. A human hand is not a parallel gripper, and the camera viewpoint, the kinematics, the force profiles are all different. So this data teaches you what to do and roughly how objects respond, but it does not directly tell you how to command your particular robot.

The way I think about it is as a funnel. Human data gives you breadth and semantic coverage of the task space. Simulation gives you volume and lets you stress-test robustness. Real-robot data, even if it is a small fraction of the total, is what grounds everything and closes the loop on your specific hardware. If I had to pick a ratio, the real-robot portion might be only a few percent, but it is the few percent you cannot skip.

What I would caution against is the belief that any single source will scale its way to generality. The internet gave vision and language models an essentially free, embodied-agnostic corpus. Robotics does not have that. We have to construct the corpus deliberately, and the design choice of how you mix these three sources is, in my view, as important as the model architecture itself.

r001.rationale: The response describes people demonstrating tasks directly in real homes, calls them highly efficient, and contrasts this with the cost of robot-based data collection. This conveys that home demonstrations can be more efficient than bringing robots into homes.

r002.rationale: The response says real-robot data grounds the other sources, closes the loop on specific hardware, and is a small share that “you cannot skip,” expressing an ongoing need for it.

astra-6.text:
I think they’re complementary. Simulation gives you scale and control: you can vary the environment, repeat experiments, and explore situations that would be expensive to reproduce on a real robot. Data collected directly with human hands captures a wide range of everyday interactions and how people accomplish tasks. But neither automatically tells you what will work on a particular robot, with its own sensors, actuators, and physical constraints.

Real-robot data closes that loop. It exposes the details that are difficult to model—contact, friction, delays, and the way small errors accumulate during execution. It also lets you test whether what you learned from the other sources actually transfers.

So I wouldn’t frame it as choosing one source. The interesting question is how to use simulation and human data to learn broadly, then use real-robot experience efficiently to adapt and correct. You want each source to contribute what it does best.

r001.rationale: The response discusses human-hand data and real-robot data generally, but does not mention collecting data in people’s homes or compare its efficiency with bringing robots into homes.

r002.rationale: The response describes real-robot data as useful for testing transfer and adapting or correcting, but does not state that it will remain necessary in the future.

sol-6.1.text:
I see them as complementary. Simulation gives us scale and lets us explore a wide range of situations. Data collected directly with human hands can capture the richness of how people interact with the world. But real-robot data tells us what actually works on the hardware, with its particular sensors, actuators, and physical constraints.

For example, a human demonstration can show what a successful manipulation looks like, but it doesn’t automatically tell a robot how much force to apply or how to recover when an object slips. Simulation can help us practice those behaviors, but its assumptions still need to be checked against reality.

So I wouldn’t frame this as choosing one source over the others. The question is how to combine them, and where real-robot experience adds the most value. We should use it both to learn behaviors and to identify the gaps that the other data sources aren’t covering.

r001.rationale: The response discusses human demonstrations generally, but does not mention collecting data in people’s homes or say that this could be more efficient than bringing robots into homes.

r002.rationale: It describes the value of real-robot data and checking assumptions against reality, but does not express a belief that real-robot data will remain necessary in the future.
